title: Pride And Prejudice: CHAPTER XVI
enhanced_title: Chapter XVI: Elizabeth's Enchantment with Mr. Wickham
author: Jane Austen
description: In Chapter 16 of Pride and Prejudice, the Bennet sisters visit their aunt Mrs. Philips in Meryton, where Elizabeth meets the charming Mr. Wickham. Through their intimate conversation, Wickham reveals the history of his grievances against Mr. Darcy, painting a picture of unjust treatment that solidifies Elizabeth's prejudice against the proud gentleman and captivates her imagination.

analysis_entries.paragraph: This chapter serves as a pivotal moment in the narrative, as Elizabeth's first substantial conversation with Mr. Wickham establishes the foundation for her prejudice against Mr. Darcy that will persist throughout much of the novel. The setting at Mrs. Philips's house provides an intimate backdrop where gossip and personal revelations flourish, allowing Wickham to present himself as a wronged innocent. Austen signals the danger of this dynamic through Elizabeth's own admission that she 'dared not even mention that gentleman,' yet Wickham raises the subject himself—a detail that should alert the reader even as it escapes Elizabeth's notice.

She dared not even
mention that gentleman.

analysis_entries.paragraph: Mr. Collins's behavior throughout the gathering demonstrates Austen's masterful use of dramatic irony and satire. His fawning admiration of Lady Catherine's grandeur, his ignorance of his own ridiculousness at the card table, and his tone-deaf comparisons reveal the absurdity of sycophantic social climbing. At the same time, Collins functions as an unwitting foil to the more subtle Wickham: where Collins's self-importance is transparent and comic, Wickham's self-presentation is polished and persuasive, making him far more dangerous.

Austen carefully contrasts Wickham's apparent openness with Darcy's reserve, creating a false dichotomy that Elizabeth and the reader must later dismantle. Wickham's willingness to share 'private' grievances immediately upon acquaintance should signal impropriety, yet Elizabeth interprets it as proof of his trustworthiness and the depth of his suffering. The irony is compounded by the narrator's observation that Elizabeth 'listened with all her heart'—her emotional engagement actively suppressing the critical faculty she elsewhere prides herself upon.

analysis_entries.paragraph: The revelation of familial connections—particularly that Lady Catherine de Bourgh is Mr. Darcy's aunt—introduces crucial structural elements that will become significant in later chapters. This knowledge reframes Collins's connection to Darcy and illuminates the intersecting social networks that constrain and complicate the characters' relationships. Elizabeth's amused thought of 'poor Miss Bingley' upon hearing that Darcy may be destined for Miss de Bourgh further demonstrates how social intelligence circulates through gossip and private conversation in Austen's world.

Wickham's account of being denied the living at Pemberley represents a sophisticated manipulation of class resentment and emotional appeal. By framing his grievance around filial duty, broken promises, and social injustice, he ensures sympathy while remaining strategically vague about specific wrongdoings that might be verified or disproved. His claim that 'there was just such an informality in the terms of the bequest as to give me no hope from law' conveniently forecloses any avenue of objective scrutiny, leaving Elizabeth with only his word against Darcy's.

analysis_entries.paragraph: The parallel drawn between Mr. Bingley's apparent goodness and his mysterious friendship with Darcy creates narrative tension and deepens Elizabeth's confusion. Wickham's explanation—that Darcy 'can please where he chooses' and is a 'very different man' among his social equals—introduces a more nuanced portrait of Darcy than Elizabeth is prepared to accept. This contrast suggests that human character resists simple categorization, a theme central to the novel's exploration of pride, prejudice, and the difficulty of true moral judgment.
analysis_entries.anchor_text_end_of_sentence: Mr. Darcy can please where he chooses.

analysis_entries.paragraph: Lydia's obsession with lottery tickets and fish serves as counterpoint to Elizabeth's absorption in Wickham's story, revealing different manifestations of feminine desire and risk-taking in Regency society. While Lydia gambles openly and noisily for material prizes, Elizabeth risks her judgment and reputation on Wickham's unverified tales—a wager she will come to regret. The closing image of the carriage ride home, in which 'neither Lydia nor Mr. Collins were once silent,' traps Elizabeth's new infatuation inside a comic frame, hinting that her enchantment is not as serious or well-founded as she believes.

summary: Chapter XVI of Pride and Prejudice marks a crucial turning point in Elizabeth Bennet's emotional and intellectual journey. During a visit to her aunt Mrs. Philips in Meryton, she engages in extended conversation with the handsome and apparently agreeable Mr. Wickham, who reveals that he has suffered grievous wrongs at the hands of Mr. Darcy. Wickham's narrative—that Darcy denied him a promised church living out of jealousy and pride—confirms Elizabeth's existing dislike of the proud gentleman and transforms it into active disdain. Meanwhile, Mr. Collins bores the company with accounts of Lady Catherine's grandeur and loses at whist without his dignity suffering. The chapter establishes Wickham as a sympathetic figure and Darcy as a villain in Elizabeth's mind, setting up the central conflict that will only be resolved when Elizabeth learns the truth about both men. Austen masterfully shows how Elizabeth's intelligence and perceptiveness can be clouded by her willingness to believe the worst of those she already dislikes and the best of those who flatter her judgment.
